analysis.title: Macro Picture: Wargaming The AI Crash
key_insights: TS Lombard models an AI-bust scenario and expects a mild US recession, comparable in size to 1990 and 2001, because the Fed has room to cut and lower rates would revive the bottom of the K-shaped economy.
US tech companies are investing about $1 trillion a year in the AI buildout. Revenue hurdle-rate studies put the needed AI revenue at $2.5-3.0 trillion by 2030, about 14 times today's level.

The firm's sustainability metric, the ratio of internal to external ecosystem revenues, is little changed since its June note. Earnings growth is still mostly recycled capex and circular financing, which leaves the boom exposed to any capex slowdown.

In the crash scenario the S&P 500 falls 30%, tech falls 40% and other sectors fall 20%. That wipes out about $20 trillion of market cap and returns tech's share of the US market to pre-ChatGPT levels.

Debt is now the marginal source of AI funding. AI companies are expected to issue about $700 billion of bonds in 2027, of which $400 billion is from hyperscalers. Off-balance-sheet liabilities are estimated at $1.5-2 trillion.

Meta's $30 billion Hyperion data center was 80% sold to Brown Owl in a joint venture, Beignet, that raised $27 billion of debt backed by Meta's 20-year leaseback. The leases are split into five four-year leases, so little of the liability shows on Meta's balance sheet.

Accounting flatters AI balance sheets. Depreciation only starts when data centers enter service, and lab lease commitments only start when capacity is live, so costs rise just as revenue expectations are tested.
Anthropic and OpenAI IPOs are flagged as a possible late-cycle signal because insiders can sell. OpenAI's IPO has been postponed to 2027.

NVIDIA is described as the barometer for the AI boom. Vendor financing and possible double and triple ordering raise the risk that shortages turn into a glut if demand slows. A BIS study is cited as finding more than 55% of incoming AI-firm investment comes from other AI firms.

Public opposition to AI is a regulatory risk. About 55% of Americans want AI development to slow, versus 13% who do not. A serious AI-linked security incident could trigger a regulatory backlash, especially after the midterms.

The key risk is the second derivative. AI capex does not need to fall to cause stress, it only needs to grow more slowly, because hyperscaler capex works like a loan book that funds the rest of the ecosystem.

Estimated credit losses on AI debt are $125-190 billion on a roughly $2.9 trillion debt stock. About 25% of the stock is assumed vulnerable, with a 35% cumulative default rate over 2028-30 and 25-50% recovery. The firm calls this material but not systemic.

Hyperscalers are not seen as the main credit risk. Distress would concentrate in neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Oracle, standalone model developers (OpenAI, Anthropic), single-asset project vehicles and equipment suppliers.

The AI crash would cut about 2 percentage points from the level of US GDP. Data-center imports offset much of the capex drop. About 800k jobs could be lost, adding about 50bps to unemployment before wider effects.

The firm finds little evidence of wealth effects on consumption. The link between net wealth and the savings rate broke down after 2016, and equity wealth is concentrated among high earners with low marginal propensity to consume.

Government bonds should rally in an AI bust. It would be a demand shock, unlike the supply-driven 1970s recessions when yields rose, and the bond-equity correlation would turn more negative. A return to ZIRP or permanent QE is not expected because the recession is mild.
Non-US equities should outperform over time. Korea and Taiwan would be hit hard, but exposure to AI is low elsewhere, unlike Dotcom when all developed markets participated.
The firm expects the dollar to weaken in an AI crash, unlike the global financial crisis. The destruction would be centered on the US, which would push funds to the euro, yen and possibly sterling.
The working assumption is that the AI capex boom ends in early 2028, but the date could slip. Shorting US tech or adding duration too early would underperform.

The recommended positioning is a diversified portfolio of global stocks at normal risk, following GMO's Ben Inker on 'easy' versus 'hard' bubbles. Add duration gradually as stress appears in the riskier parts of the AI ecosystem.
The firm says its hawkish Fed view is now mostly priced in. The report states the Fed is hiking rates and bond yields are rising.

sector_views.rationale: Tech is about 40% of US market cap and semiconductors near 20%. An AI bust would hit tech hardest, with a 40% fall in the scenario.
A diversified global portfolio offers normal risk and should hold up better in a crash because exposure to AI is low outside the US, Korea and Taiwan.
Yields should fall in a demand-shock recession. The firm advises adding duration over time as AI stress signs emerge.

earnings_insights: US tech trailing PE is about 30, down from 40 a year ago and below the 70-75 Dotcom-era peak. The report questions whether the 'E' is sustainable, because earnings rely on recycled capex.
The 'other' category of hyperscaler revenues is described as largely valuation gains on crossholdings in other AI companies, and would take a hit in a crash.

In the scenario, hyperscalers face serious revenue downgrades, and lower capex would offer little consolation. Their balance sheets are strong, so the main risk is to earnings and asset valuations, not debt.

trade_ideas.description: Hold a diversified portfolio of global equities at normal risk instead of concentrated US tech exposure
trade_ideas.rationale: Should do well if the boom continues and outperform in a crash, following GMO's Ben Inker on hard versus easy bubbles.
trade_ideas.risk: Initial indiscriminate risk-off selling in a crash would hit all equities, and Korea and Taiwan would be hit hardest.

trade_ideas.description: Add government bond duration gradually as signs of stress appear in the riskier parts of the AI ecosystem
trade_ideas.rationale: An AI bust would be a demand shock that lowers long-term yields, unlike 1970s supply shocks.
trade_ideas.risk: Adding duration too early underperforms while yields keep grinding higher during the boom.

trade_ideas.description: Expect a weaker dollar over time versus the euro, yen and possibly sterling in an AI crash
trade_ideas.rationale: Destruction would be centered on the US financial system, which pushes funds to other jurisdictions, and holders would not need US Treasurys for safety.
trade_ideas.risk: A classic risk-off reaction could briefly support the dollar, and the dollar was little moved in the first 18 months of the Dotcom crash.

risk_factors: AI revenues fall short of the hurdle rate and are concentrated, with 80% of OpenAI and Anthropic earnings coming from 1% of customers.
Credit taps could be turned off by lenders outside the AI ecosystem, with borrowing costs and junk spreads rising. CoreWeave is cited as paying about 15% interest.
Accounting teaser effects: the depreciation cliff and lab lease commitments starting only when data centers go live.
IPO lockup expirations and insider selling could signal a top.
NVIDIA disappointment, vendor financing and a semiconductor bullwhip effect.
Regulatory and safety backlash after a serious AI-related incident.
AI-driven automation during a downturn could worsen the labour market hit and cause a jobless recovery.
Confidence and reflexivity effects could make the recession worse than the mild baseline.
charts_described: Chart 1 compares cumulative investment as a percent of GDP for datacenters against US Railroads, the Interstate Highway System, the Marshall Plan, Apollo and the Manhattan Project, with the railway boom reaching under 200% over 70 years.
Chart 6 shows AI ecosystem revenues and the recycled capex share, with revenues from outside the ecosystem still small.
Chart 12 shows tech share of the US stock market, reported in the text as near 40%.
Chart 20 compares a hypothetical AI recession in 2028 with the 1981, 1990, 2001 and 2008 real GDP paths, and the text says it is roughly on a par with 1990 and 2001.
vol_and_positioning: TS Lombard clients are mostly fully invested and nobody is shorting US tech, following the Soros principle of buying a forming bubble.
Markets have been jittery in recent weeks, and the report says it is unclear whether this is the start of the AI bust or will blow over.
Shorting tech or adding duration too early risks a period of underperformance if the boom continues, so positioning timing is the main problem.
geopolitical: The report mentions an energy crisis that investors hope will end, which would help global equities if the AI boom continues.
US-China competition: open-weight Chinese models are gaining market share and could commoditize AI.
US midterms: politics may turn less tech-friendly afterward, raising regulatory risk.
cross_bank_references: The report cites revenue hurdle-rate estimates from Goldman, The Economist, Van Nieuwerburgh, and Bernstein and Cummings.
The firm disagrees with Julien Garran's claim that the AI buildout is the biggest misallocation of capital in history.
The firm agrees with Ben Inker of GMO on trading easy versus hard bubbles.
The firm notes the IMF's latest WEO estimates of the GDP hit are similar to its own.

tension_points.bull_case: Tech earnings and revenues keep rising, keeping the bull thesis intact, and PE ratios of about 30 are far below Dotcom peaks. Clients are fully invested and say frontier AI is good enough to matter.
tension_points.bear_case: Revenue is mostly recycled capex and circular financing, with AI revenue needing about a 14x rise to meet hurdle rates. Funding is shifting to debt, and vendor financing and off-balance-sheet structures are growing.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A slowdown in the growth rate of hyperscaler capex, an NVIDIA disappointment, or a shift of credit markets to cut funding would end the boom. The report assumes the end comes in early 2028.

tension_points.bull_case: The recession would be mild, comparable to 1990 and 2001. Private balance sheets are healthy, the Fed has room to cut, and lower rates would revive the bottom of the K-shaped economy.
tension_points.bear_case: Confidence effects, reflexive job losses and AI-driven automation during a downturn could deepen the hit and produce a jobless recovery.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Employment starting to contract and triggering reflexive spending cuts, or a wave of AI automation layoffs during the downturn, would invalidate the mild-recession view.
